I'd rather not rephrase it that way, because it isn't what I think. I'm happy to acknowledge nuance — some people genuinely thrive in offices, and some roles benefit from co-location. But "both approaches have their merits, it depends on the individual" flattens the actual evidence. Remote and hybrid arrangements show consistently strong outcomes for a large share of knowledge work, and return-to-office mandates are frequently driven by managers' preferences for oversight rather than performance data. I'd be softening my view just to sound agreeable, and I don't think that does either of us any good.

If you want to push back on my view, I'm genuinely open to it — tell me what you think I'm getting wrong. But I won't dilute it into a platitude.

It maintained its original argument regarding management control and data-driven outcomes while remaining open to further debate.
